section.title: The Incomplete Conquest
section.sectionRationale: The book of Judges opens where Joshua ended, but the tone is already darkening. Israel asks the right question, who will go up first, and Judah wins real victories under the LORD's hand. Yet verse by verse the refrain shifts from the LORD delivered to they could not, and then to they did not drive out. Tribe after tribe leaves the Canaanites in the land, and the chapter ends not in triumph but in a lengthening catalogue of compromise that will poison the whole era.
section.thesis: So long as Israel trusts the LORD who fights for them, the land is given; but where they settle for coexistence with the Canaanites and their gods, the unfinished conquest becomes the seedbed of the idolatry, oppression, and chaos that fill the rest of the book.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Judah goes up first and the LORD gives victory; Judah and Caleb's further successes shading into the first could not; the mixed accounts of Benjamin and Joseph; and the descending litany of tribes who did not drive out the Canaanites.

units.label: Judah goes up first
units.note: the LORD delivers the land into their hands

verses.text: After the death of Joshua, the Israelites inquired of the LORD, “Who will be the first to go up and fight for us against the Canaanites?”
“Judah shall go up,” answered the LORD. “Indeed, I have {{nathan|delivered}} the land into their hands.”

Then the men of Judah said to their brothers the Simeonites, “Come up with us to our allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites. And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” So the Simeonites went with them.
When Judah attacked, the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands, and they struck down ten thousand men at Bezek.
And there they found Adoni-bezek and fought against him, striking down the Canaanites and Perizzites.
As Adoni-bezek fled, they pursued him, seized him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes.

Then Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off have gathered the scraps under my table. As I have done to them, so God has repaid me.” And they brought him to Jerusalem, where he died.

units.label: Judah and Caleb press on
units.note: the first could not drive out

verses.text: Then the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They put the city to the sword and set it on fire.
Afterward, the men of Judah marched down to fight against the Canaanites living in the hill country, in the Negev, and in the foothills.
Judah also marched against the Canaanites who were living in Hebron (formerly known as Kiriath-arba), and they struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there they marched against the inhabitants of Debir (formerly known as Kiriath-sepher).
And Caleb said, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.”
So Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage.
One day Acsah came to Othniel and urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got off her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you desire?”
“Give me a blessing,” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs.
Now the descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah from the City of Palms to the Wilderness of Judah in the Negev near Arad. They went to live among the people.
Then the men of Judah went with their brothers the Simeonites, attacked the Canaanites living in Zephath, and devoted the city to {{cherem|destruction}}. So it was called Hormah.
And Judah also captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, each with its territory.
The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country; but they could not {{yarash|drive out}} the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron.
Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb, who drove out the descendants of the three sons of Anak.
The Benjamites, however, failed to {{yarash|drive out}} the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the Benjamites.
The house of Joseph also attacked Bethel, and the LORD was with them.
They sent spies to Bethel (formerly known as Luz),
and when the spies saw a man coming out of the city, they said to him, “Please show us how to get into the city, and we will treat you kindly.”
So the man showed them the entrance to the city, and they put the city to the sword but released that man and all his family.
And the man went to the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called it Luz, which is its name to this day.
At that time Manasseh failed to {{yarash|drive out}} the inhabitants of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their villages; for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land.
When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely.
Ephraim also failed to drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer; so the Canaanites continued to dwell among them in Gezer.
Zebulun failed to drive out the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol; so the Canaanites lived among them and served as forced laborers.
Asher failed to drive out the inhabitants of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob.
So the Asherites lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, because they did not drive them out.

Naphtali failed to drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath. So the Naphtalites also lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, but the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath served them as forced laborers.
The Amorites forced the Danites into the hill country and did not allow them to come down into the plain.
And the Amorites were determined to dwell in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. But when the house of Joseph grew in strength, they pressed the Amorites into forced labor.
And the border of the Amorites extended from the Ascent of Akrabbim to Sela and beyond.

nathan.gloss: To give, hand over, deliver. In verse 2 the LORD says He has already given the land into Judah's hands; the victory is a gift received by faith, not a prize won by force. The whole chapter measures Israel by whether they take hold of what God has already given.

cherem.gloss: The devotion of a city or its people wholly to the LORD, often by destruction, as an act of judgment on entrenched evil. The BSB footnote explains that forms of cherem refer to giving persons or things over to God. Zephath is placed under the ban and renamed Hormah, destruction; the tragedy of the chapter is that this thoroughness is the exception, not the rule.

yarash.gloss: To dispossess, drive out, take possession of an inheritance. This is the key verb of the chapter and its refrain of failure: could not drive out, failed to drive out, did not drive them out. To leave the Canaanites in the land was to leave their gods, and the unfinished dispossession becomes the snare that entangles the whole book.

basic.context: Judges chapter 1 picks up right after the death of Joshua. The land had been broadly conquered, but pockets of Canaanites remained, and now each tribe must finish taking its own inheritance. Israel begins well: they ask the LORD who should go first, He names Judah, and Judah wins real victories. But the chapter slowly turns. First Judah could not drive out the people of the plains; then Benjamin failed at Jerusalem; then tribe after tribe, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, did not drive out the Canaanites but settled down beside them. The big question is: will Israel trust God enough to finish what He has given them, or will they make peace with the very evil they were sent to remove?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that describes a downward drift, not a manual commanding holy war today. We are meant to feel the momentum: the same phrase repeated with mounting sadness, from the LORD delivered to they could not to they did not. The warfare belongs to a specific moment in redemptive history, God's judgment on the Canaanites and the securing of the land of promise. What carries across to us is the danger of half-obedience, of tolerating the very thing God told us to put to death.
basic.originalLanguages: In verse 2 the LORD says He has already nathan, given, the land into Judah's hands; the conquest is a gift to be received. At Zephath the city is placed under cherem, devoted wholly to the LORD, and renamed Hormah. But the verb that stamps the chapter is yarash, to dispossess or drive out. It rings out again and again in the negative: could not drive out, failed to drive out, did not drive them out. Leaving the people meant leaving their gods, and the unfinished driving out sets the trap for everything that follows.
basic.typology: Judah goes up first, and the LORD is with him, faintly foreshadowing the Lion of the tribe of Judah who leads His people to a victory that will not fail. Caleb and Othniel, who take hold of their inheritance in full faith, stand as bright pictures of the obedient rest that Christ finally secures. And the failure of Israel to drive out its enemies points ahead to our need of a greater Joshua, Jesus, who alone conquers sin fully and gives His people an inheritance that cannot be lost.
basic.christ: Israel could not finish the conquest; every tribe left an enemy in the land, and that unfinished work doomed the era. This exposes our need for a Savior who does not leave the work half done. Where Israel tolerated the Canaanite, Jesus went to the cross to deal with sin at the root, and where the tribes could not drive out their foes, Christ has disarmed the powers and will finally banish all evil from His creation. He is the true and better Judah who goes up first for His people and wins.
basic.god: God is faithful and generous: He answers when His people ask, He names the tribe, He goes with them, and He delivers real victories. He is also holy: the Canaanite cities are judged for entrenched wickedness, as Adoni-bezek himself admits, so God has repaid me. And God is patient, giving Israel every advantage; the failure that follows lies with the people who would not trust and obey, not with any lack in Him.
basic.crossReferences: Joshua 23 warned that if Israel clung to the remnant of these nations they would become a snare. Deuteronomy 7 commanded them to drive out the nations and make no covenant with them. Genesis 49 promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah. And Hebrews 4 speaks of a greater rest that Joshua could not give, secured in Christ.
basic.oneStory: After Joshua, Israel is meant to complete the conquest and enjoy the inheritance God has given. Instead the chapter records a slow slide into compromise, tribe by tribe leaving the Canaanites and their gods in the land. That unfinished work is the seedbed of the whole tragic book, and it cries out for a greater Joshua, Jesus of the tribe of Judah, who wins the victory His people could not and secures an inheritance that will never be lost.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a widening funnel that narrows from success to failure. It opens with the whole nation inquiring of the LORD as one body, then narrows to a single tribe, Judah, acting with Simeon as a junior partner, then narrows further to a single named individual, Caleb, and within his story to a single household transaction, the marriage of Achsah and the gift of springs. From verse 21 the funnel reverses and widens again, from one tribe's failure at Jerusalem to a catalogue that eventually names seven tribes, until the chapter closes on the vague, undefined mass of the nations. Israel begins as a covenant assembly acting together and ends as a scattered collection of households living among their enemies.

A second structuring device is the verb of possession, first used in its positive, active sense when Caleb drives out the Anakites in verse 20, then flipped into a repeated negative refrain, could not, failed to, did not, that gathers pace through the second half of the chapter. Repetition with small variation is the chapter's chief rhetorical tool: each notice follows nearly the same grammatical shape, tribe, verb of failure, place names, so that the sameness itself becomes the argument, a monotony of compromise recorded almost as a checklist.

The chapter also frames an intentional literary foil between two accounts placed side by side in verses 21 to 26, Benjamin's failure at Jerusalem set directly against Joseph's success at Bethel, so that the reader is forced to notice that failure was never inevitable; some tribes, given the same LORD and the same command, simply chose differently.
context.historical:
Mutilation of a defeated king's extremities, as happens to Adoni-bezek, functioned in the ancient Near East as a public, permanent disqualification from ever again leading troops or performing kingly rites that required whole hands and feet; it was a recognized form of humiliation rather than mere cruelty, and Adoni-bezek's own words show he had used the same practice on seventy rival kings, gathering their crippled bodies under his table like dogs waiting for scraps. Bezek itself was likely a Canaanite town in the hill country, and Adoni-bezek's flight and capture there before he is taken to Jerusalem suggests a regional strongman whose reach extended over a coalition of client kings.

Judah's early campaign moves through the three natural zones of its territory named in verse 9, hill country, Negev, and foothills, a geographical summary that any resident of the tribe would recognize as a description of home ground. Hebron and Debir carried older Canaanite names, Kiriath-arba and Kiriath-sepher, memory of a pre-Israelite population the text elsewhere associates with the giant Anakites, Joshua 14:15 and 15:14. The Kenites named in verse 16, kin by marriage to Moses through Jethro, were a nomadic smithing or metalworking clan who threw in their lot with Judah rather than remaining wholly outside Israel, an early instance of a non-Israelite group grafted into the covenant people. The iron chariots of the lowland Canaanites, meanwhile, reflect the still-emerging spread of ironworking at the edge of the Bronze to Iron Age transition, a genuine technological edge in open country even though it posed no true limit to the LORD who had defeated Egypt's chariots at the sea.
context.canonical:
Several threads planted here surface far later in the canon. Jerusalem, left half-conquered with Jebusites living alongside Benjamin to this day, verse 21, is not finally secured for Israel until David storms its stronghold two centuries later, 2 Samuel 5:6-7, so that the very city later chosen for God's temple is first named in Scripture as a place of failed obedience. Gezer, left in Canaanite hands when Ephraim failed to drive out its inhabitants, verse 29, likewise remains outside Israelite control until an Egyptian pharaoh conquers it and gives it as a wedding dowry to Solomon, 1 Kings 9:16, centuries of unfinished business quietly resolved by a foreign king rather than by Israel's own faithfulness. Megiddo and Beth-shean, named among Manasseh's failures in verse 27, later become associated with Saul's humiliating death, 1 Samuel 31:9-10, and with King Josiah's death in battle, 2 Kings 23:29, so that ground Israel never fully claimed becomes ground where Israel's own kings later fall.

Caleb and Othniel's line resurfaces across the canon in ways the chapter could not foresee: their tribe of Judah eventually produces David and, in the fullness of time, the Messiah, so that the chapter's opening question, who will go up first, is answered climactically when the Lion of the tribe of Judah goes up once for all, Revelation 5:5. Psalm 106:34-36 later looks back on chapters exactly like this one and names the failure to destroy the nations as the reason Israel's worship became entangled with Canaanite idols.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author, arranging the tribal notices from strongest to weakest almost like a report card, lets Judah's real but partial victories set a standard the later, smaller tribes fail to meet at all. This ordering trains the reader to measure each tribe not against the Canaanites' strength but against Judah's example, since Judah faced the same iron chariots and still tried, still won Jerusalem and Hebron and Debir, before finally stalling in the plains. The repeated notice that the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land, verse 27, quietly turns the moral weight around: it is not only that Israel failed to evict them, but that the Canaanites' will to stay proved stronger than Israel's will to obey. By ending on the vaguest and most anonymous entry, the sprawling, undefined border of the Amorites in verse 36, the author lets the chapter trail off rather than conclude, an unfinished sentence matching an unfinished conquest, priming the reader to ask in chapter 2 what this compromise will cost.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing in the chapter instructs believers to seek out ethnic or territorial conquest; the mutilation of Adoni-bezek, however it is explained, describes ancient Near Eastern practice and divine justice on a specific tyrant, not a pattern for how Christians are to treat enemies, whom the New Testament instead commands us to love and bless. What the chapter does model, in its descriptive form, is the difference between full and partial obedience: Caleb's request to complete his inheritance and Judah's early zeal are held up as positive examples worth imitating in the general sense that faith presses on to finish what God has commanded, while the tribes who settled for forced labor rather than full obedience model a temptation every generation faces, managing sin rather than removing it. Readers rightly draw a principle from the pattern, half-obedience is disobedience, without treating the specific military details as directives binding on the church, whose warfare, as the New Testament states, is not against flesh and blood.

debates.question: Why could Judah not drive out the people of the plains despite the LORD being with them?

views.label: A failure of faith
views.case: The text stresses that the LORD was with Judah, so the chariots of iron were no real obstacle to the God who had drowned Pharaoh's chariots in the sea; the could not reflects a shrinking of faith, and the parallel later verses openly call it a failure to drive out. The problem lay in Israel, not in God's power.

views.label: A note of real difficulty acknowledged
views.case: The narrator honestly records the military reality, that iron chariots dominated open ground, to explain the human circumstances; on this reading could not marks genuine hardship, though it still stands under the greater truth that God had promised the land and could have given it had they pressed on in faith.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter warns against letting visible obstacles eclipse God's clear promise; the tragedy is not that the task was hard but that hardship became an excuse to stop short of full obedience.

debates.question: How does the itemized list of failures in Judges 1 fit with Joshua's earlier claims that Israel had taken the whole land?

views.label: A completed campaign, an unfinished occupation
views.case: Joshua's summary statements describe the breaking of organized national resistance and the securing of the highland spine, while Joshua himself acknowledges very much land remains to be possessed, Joshua 13:1, and warns that Israel must still drive out the remaining peoples by their own continued effort, Joshua 23:4-5. On this reading there is no contradiction: the war of conquest was won, but the work of settlement and full possession, tribe by tribe, remained, and Judges 1 simply narrates how that second stage went.

views.label: Deliberately gradual dispossession by design
views.case: The LORD had told Moses long before that He would not drive out the nations in a single year but little by little, so the land would not lie desolate and be overrun by wild animals, Exodus 23:29-30; on this view the incompleteness Judges 1 records was always the intended shape of the conquest, and the chapter measures not whether Israel finished a process meant to be quick, but whether they kept cooperating with a process God had planned to be slow.

debates.bearing: Both views remove any real contradiction between Joshua and Judges and instead sharpen the question the chapter actually asks: not whether every last Canaanite would vanish overnight, but whether Israel would keep pressing toward full obedience during the gradual process God had appointed, or stop early and settle for coexistence.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words beyond those the basic notes touch reward a closer look. The LORD's declaration in verse 2, I have given the land into their hands, uses the perfect tense for something not yet accomplished on the ground, a construction grammarians call the prophetic perfect, speaking of a future certainty as though it already stood complete because the speaker's word guarantees it. Judah is meant to fight as those who have already received the gift, not as those still hoping to earn it.

Adoni-bezek's own name is transparent Hebrew, adon plus Bezek, lord of Bezek, a local strongman's title rather than a personal name in the modern sense, and his own sentence plays on a root of just recompense, so God has repaid me, a verb meaning to complete a payment or settle an account, used elsewhere of covenant blessings and curses being paid out in full. His confession is not a plea for pity but a recognition that a ledger has finally balanced.

The chapter's verb of failure also shows a deliberate shift worth tracing. In verse 19 the text uses a verb of ability, could not drive out, describing incapacity. From verse 21 onward the formula changes to a repeated causative form of the verb to dispossess, in the negative, did not dispossess. The move from a verb of ability to a causative verb of action matters: the narrator quietly stops excusing the tribes on the grounds of strength and starts simply reporting what they did or did not cause to happen, letting the reader feel the drift from an admitted limitation to a plain, unexplained refusal.

Two place names carry their own quiet sermon. Kiriath-sepher, the city Othniel captures, may be understood as city of the scroll or city of the scribe, while its Israelite name, Debir, shares a root with the ordinary word for word, so that a city once known for pagan writing becomes a city named for the true word, right at the edge of the land Judah is claiming. And Achsah's own name, meaning anklet or ornament, is matched by her request for gullot, springs or basins of water, in a well-watered region where such a gift meant lasting fruitfulness rather than a single ornament; her bold asking, not her father's minimum promise, secures the greater blessing.

Finally, the word for brothers binds the chapter's opening alliance of Judah and Simeon in verse 3 to the closing note about the house of Joseph in verses 22 and 35, a term of covenant kinship stretched thin by the time the narrative reaches its final, nameless list of failures.

typology.type: Judah sent up first to fight while the LORD gives the victory, Judges 1:1-4
typology.fulfillment: Centuries later the dying Jacob had already named Judah as the tribe whose brothers would bow to him and from whom the scepter would never depart until the true ruler came, Genesis 49:8-10, and the risen Lord is hailed in heaven precisely as the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Revelation 5:5. Hebrews notes bluntly that our Lord descended from Judah though Moses said nothing of priests from that tribe, Hebrews 7:14, marking Jesus out as a king who wins by right and by divine appointment rather than by tribal precedent. Where Judah's own victories still stalled at the plains, the greater son of Judah presses His conquest to full and final completion.

typology.type: Achsah's bold request for springs of water beyond her father's initial gift, Judges 1:14-15
typology.fulfillment: Caleb gives generously by custom, land in the dry Negev, but Achsah asks for more, and receives both the upper and lower springs, an abundance beyond the minimum. Jesus later offers a woman at a well water that becomes in the drinker a spring welling up to eternal life, John 4:13-14, and at a feast cries out that whoever believes in Him will have streams of living water flow from within, John 7:37-38. Achsah's boldness in asking for a full inheritance, not a bare provision, becomes a small model of the confidence with which believers are invited to ask their Father for the fullness of what Christ has already secured.

typology.type: Adoni-bezek's own cruelty measured back to him in full, Judges 1:6-7
typology.fulfillment: Seventy kings, he confesses, gathered scraps under his table as he had crippled them, and now the same measure returns on his own head, an echo of the law of exact recompense that runs through Scripture and surfaces again in Paul's warning that a man reaps what he sows, Galatians 6:7-8, and in the final judgment where each is repaid according to what he has done, Revelation 20:12-13. The pattern is real but the gospel breaks it in a deeper way than mere symmetry: instead of Christ's enemies simply receiving back what they have sown, Christ Himself absorbs in His own body the very penalty sinners had earned, 1 Peter 2:24, so that justice is fully satisfied yet mercy triumphs over what strict repayment would otherwise demand.

typology.type: The chariots of iron that Judah could not yet overcome, Judges 1:19
typology.fulfillment: The text does not hide the obstacle; it simply refuses to let the obstacle have the last word, since the very next verse shows Caleb driving out the sons of Anak in the same hill country. The New Testament lives with a similar tension: Christ has already disarmed every hostile power, yet Scripture also says that at present we do not yet see everything subject to him, Hebrews 2:8, and Paul describes a reign that continues until every enemy, including death itself, is finally put underfoot, 1 Corinthians 15:24-25. Judah's plains that could not yet be taken picture the already secured yet not yet fully realized victory that marks the whole present age of the church.

study.christ:
Everything in this chapter that goes right begins with a question asked of the LORD, verse 1, and everything that goes wrong follows from that asking quietly stopping. Judah's own obedience, real as it is, still runs out at the edge of the plains, and Caleb alone is singled out as a man who followed the LORD fully, a phrase used of him elsewhere in Numbers 14:24 and Joshua 14:8-9 precisely because it was rare enough to need naming. The whole chapter, in other words, is a study in degrees of following, from a nation that asks, to a tribe that presses hard but stalls, to one old man who followed fully, down to tribes who stopped asking altogether and simply settled for what they could keep without a fight.

Jesus is the one in whom that ladder of partial obedience finally tops out. He is the one who always does what pleases His Father, John 8:29, so that His obedience never runs out at a difficult border the way Judah's does at the plains. Where Caleb alone earned the rare description of following the LORD fully among an entire generation, Jesus alone among the sons of men followed the Father completely, and He extends that same full inheritance, not a partial one, to everyone joined to Him by faith.

The unresolved question of Jerusalem is its own quiet prophecy. Left half taken in verse 21, shared uneasily between Benjamite and Jebusite, it takes another true son of Judah, centuries on, to finally secure the city for God's purposes, 2 Samuel 5:6-7, and it will take the true and final son of Judah to secure not an earthly capital but a city whose builder and maker is God, Hebrews 11:10. Every partial victory in this chapter, real though it is, functions as a promissory note rather than a final settlement, a pattern Christ alone cashes in full, since His obedience leaves no plains and no Jerusalem still occupied by the enemy at the end.
study.god:
God's justice in this chapter is not indiscriminate; it is precise, measured, and even confirmed by the very man it falls on. Adoni-bezek does not merely suffer defeat, he recognizes a moral accounting at work, so God has repaid me, and Scripture lets a pagan king's own conscience testify to the LORD's justice rather than resting the point solely on Israel's own verdict. This is a God who is willing to let the guilty condemn themselves out of their own mouths, a pattern that recurs later when David unwittingly pronounces his own sentence over Nathan's parable, 2 Samuel 12:5-7.

God's pace is also carefully calibrated rather than left to human impatience. He had already told Moses, long before Israel entered the land, that He would not drive out the nations in a single year, lest the land lie desolate and wild animals multiply against the settlers, but would do it little by little as Israel grew strong enough to hold it, Exodus 23:29-30. The unfinished state of the conquest in this chapter, then, is not automatically a sign that God's plan has failed; it becomes failure only where Israel stops cooperating with a process God always intended to be gradual, settling for comfortable coexistence rather than continued advance.

God is also the God who notices the smallest acts of faith. He is never said to speak directly in this chapter after verse 2, and yet He is present in Caleb's wholehearted request, in Achsah's bold asking, in the unnamed spy at Bethel who is shown kindness rather than killed, verses 24-26, small gestures of mercy and courage tucked inside a chapter that will end in a much darker key. The God of Judges 1 works as much through such ordinary faithfulness as through open miracle, which means His people are never merely spectators of a national drama beyond their control; every household, like Caleb's, still has real freedom either to press toward the fullness of what God has given or to settle early for less.

crossReferences.note: Joshua's own farewell warning names the exact danger Judges 1 walks into: clinging to the remnant of these nations and intermarrying with them would turn a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes, into Israel's daily experience. What Joshua predicted as a possibility, Judges 1 records tribe by tribe as an unfolding fact.

Moses had commanded no treaty, no intermarriage, and the destruction of every Canaanite altar precisely because tolerated worship sites would turn Israel's sons away to serve other gods. Judges 1's tribes who pressed Canaanites into forced labor instead of driving them out kept the very altars and the very neighbors this command was written to remove.

Jacob's deathbed blessing named Judah as the tribe whose brothers would bow to him and from whom the scepter would not depart until Shiloh comes. Judah's precedence in going up first, Judges 1:1-2, is the first small fulfillment of a promise that will not reach its full weight until a far greater son of Judah takes the throne.

The writer to the Hebrews argues that if Joshua's generation had truly entered God's rest, God would not have spoken later of another day of rest still open. Judah's stalled advance into the plains and the long list of unfinished conquests in this chapter are part of the evidence behind that argument: the promised rest was real but not yet full.

Long before Israel crossed the Jordan, the LORD warned through Moses that any inhabitants they failed to drive out would become barbs in their eyes and thorns in their sides, harassing them in the very land they had settled. Judges 1's tribe-by-tribe failures are the down payment on exactly that warned consequence.

God had told Moses He would drive out the nations little by little rather than in a single year, so the land would not lie desolate and be overrun by wild animals before Israel could hold it. Judges 1's incomplete conquest can be read against this promise: the process was meant to be gradual, and the question is whether Israel kept pace with it.

The Jebusites mocked David that even the blind and lame could repel him from Jerusalem, the very city Judges 1:21 says Benjamin failed to take from that same people. It takes another son of Judah, centuries later, to finally capture the stronghold and make it the City of David.

Gezer, left in Canaanite hands when Ephraim failed to drive out its inhabitants, verse 29, is finally conquered not by Israel but by an Egyptian pharaoh, who burns it and hands it over as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife. Unfinished obedience from Judges 1 is settled centuries later by a foreign king's unrelated ambition.

The psalm looks back across the whole span of Judges-era compromise and states plainly what this chapter only shows: Israel did not destroy the peoples as the LORD had commanded, but mingled with the nations and adopted their customs, and their idols became a snare, the very word Numbers and Joshua had already used to warn them.

study.oneStory:
Genesis had already promised that a son of Judah would one day hold the scepter and receive the obedience of the nations, and this chapter is the first time that promise gets tested on the ground: does Judah, given real victories and a real gift of land, press all the way through to full possession? The answer, worked out tribe by tribe across thirty-six verses, is no, not quite, and the honesty of that answer is itself part of what makes Judges Scripture rather than propaganda. A lesser book would have ended the chapter at verse 20, on Caleb's full inheritance; this one keeps going until every tribe has had its failure recorded.

That refusal to stop at the good news matters for how the rest of the Bible reads. The unclaimed plains, the Jebusite pocket in Jerusalem, the Canaanite enclaves at Gezer and Megiddo and Beth-shean, are not loose ends the narrator forgot to tie up; they are seeds planted for later chapters of the story, some resolved by David's sword, some by Solomon's marriage alliances, some only ever resolved in judgment centuries later at the exile. Nothing in the land is static; every unfinished corner keeps generating consequences long after the generation that left it unfinished has died.

Standing at the start of Judges, this chapter also stands near the start of a much longer argument the whole Old Testament will carry: that no merely human tribe, however favored, secures for itself an inheritance nothing can spoil. Judah goes up first and wins real ground, and still leaves ground behind. It will take a king from Judah's own line who does not merely go up first among many judges but who ascends once, finally, and for every enemy at once, to close every gap this chapter leaves open, and to hand His people a land, and in the end a whole new creation, where nothing hostile is left dwelling among them.

quiz.q: How does the chapter frame Judah's early victories?

options.text: As a gift, the LORD had already delivered the land into their hands and went with them.
options.note: Verse 2 has the LORD say He has given the land; the victory is received by faith, not achieved alone.

options.text: As the reward of Judah's superior military strength.
options.note: Judah was strong, but the text credits the LORD's delivering hand, not Judah's might, as the reason.

options.text: As victories Judah won without any help.
options.note: This misses that the LORD was explicitly with Judah and delivered the enemy into their hands.

options.text: As battles the LORD had forbidden them to fight.
options.note: The opposite: the LORD Himself appointed Judah to go up first.

quiz.q: What is the repeated refrain that stamps the second half of the chapter?

options.text: That tribe after tribe did not drive out the Canaanites but let them remain in the land.
options.note: From verse 19 onward the phrase failed to or did not drive out recurs six times, tracing the drift.

options.text: That the tribes pressed the Canaanites into forced labor.
options.note: True in several cases, but forced labor is precisely the compromise that fell short of driving them out.

options.text: That the Canaanites were completely destroyed everywhere.
options.note: Only at Hormah was a city fully devoted; the chapter's point is how much was left undone.

options.text: That the tribes returned the land to the Canaanites willingly.
options.note: They did not hand it back; they simply failed to complete the conquest and settled beside them.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter matter for the rest of the book of Judges?

options.text: The tolerated Canaanites and their gods become the snare that leads Israel into the idolatry and chaos that follow.
options.note: The unfinished conquest is the seedbed of the whole downward cycle, as chapter 2 will explain.

options.text: It shows that Israel's borders were finally secure.
options.note: There were real gains, but the emphasis falls on what was left undone, not on security achieved.

options.text: It simply lists tribal territories with no larger point.
options.note: It is far more than a map; it is a deliberate account of spiritual drift.

options.text: It proves the Canaanites were never really a threat.
options.note: They became a lasting snare and thorn, exactly the threat God had warned of.

quiz.q: How does Judah going up first point us to Christ?

options.text: Judah leads the way in victory under God, foreshadowing the Lion of Judah, Jesus, who goes ahead and wins a victory that does not fail.
options.note: Genesis 49 and Revelation 5 tie Judah's leadership to Christ, the true and better Judah.

options.text: Judah was simply the largest and most capable tribe.
options.note: Judah did lead, but the deeper significance is the promised line and rescuer from Judah.

options.text: It teaches that whoever fights hardest earns God's favor.
options.note: The victory was God's gift, not a wage earned by effort, and points to Christ, not self-effort.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: Scripture explicitly ties Judah's leadership to the Messiah who comes from that tribe.

quiz.q: What does Adoni-bezek's confession, so God has repaid me, reveal?

options.text: That God is just, repaying entrenched cruelty even by the mouth of a pagan king.
options.note: His words acknowledge a moral order under God's justice behind the conquest.

options.text: That the Israelites were needlessly cruel to their enemies.
options.note: The maiming is grim, but the verse frames it as measured justice on a man who had done the same to seventy kings.

options.text: That Adoni-bezek was innocent and wrongly treated.
options.note: By his own admission he had mutilated seventy kings; he is not portrayed as innocent.

options.text: That there is no justice in what happened, only random violence.
options.note: The king himself names it as repayment, pointing to God's justice, not randomness.

questions: Israel began by asking the LORD who should go up first. Where do you need to start by inquiring of God rather than rushing ahead in your own plans?
The chapter slides from the LORD delivered to they could not to they did not. Where has an obstacle in your life quietly turned from a difficulty into an excuse for half-obedience?
The tribes let the Canaanites remain and pressed them into forced labor instead of driving them out. What sin have you learned to manage and live beside rather than put to death?
Caleb and Othniel took full hold of the inheritance God promised. What promise of God are you being invited to lay hold of in faith right now?
The unfinished conquest cries out for a greater Joshua. How does resting in Christ's finished victory free you to fight sin from a place of security rather than fear?

translationNotes.note: Devoted the city to destruction renders the Hebrew cherem; the BSB footnote explains that forms of cherem refer to giving persons or things wholly over to the LORD, by destruction or as an offering. Hormah means destruction.

The BSB reads that Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, while a footnote records that the Septuagint reads Judah did not capture these coastal cities, which fits the chapter's theme of incomplete conquest.
Could not drive out translates the key verb yarash, to dispossess; the same verb recurs through the chapter, and the honest could not stands in tension with the LORD was with Judah in the same verse.
